name: Mixpanel
tagline: Collect a small transparent event stream and build funnels and retention locally

pricing.notes: Growth pricing is usage based; canonical monthly amount is null.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 1,000,000 events/month, 10,000 session replays/month, 5 saved reports per seat, 30 Spark AI queries/month, and unlimited seats
tiers.notes: Permanent free plan; reports become inaccessible after 1 million monthly events until upgrade or the next monthly reset.

tiers.name: Growth
tiers.limits: First 1,000,000 events/month free; selectable through 20 million events/month, 20,000 session replays/month included and configurable up to 500,000, 60 Spark AI queries/month, unlimited reports and seats
tiers.notes: Monthly starts at $0 for 1 million events. Annual purchase requires a precommit above 1 million events; the public calculator does not expose a stable minimum annual dollar amount in parsed text.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Up to 1 trillion events/month, customizable session-replay volume, 300 Spark AI queries/month, and unlimited seats/reports
tiers.notes: Event-priced Enterprise is quote only; an alternative MTU-based Enterprise contract starts at $20,000/year.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1,000,000 events/month, 10,000 session replays/month, 5 saved reports per seat, 30 Spark AI queries/month, and unlimited seats
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; annual Growth requires more than 1 million events/month committed; card charged at the start of each billing period
pricing.hiddenCosts: Growth has no billing cap: overages on the 1M-event plan are $0.00028/event and billed next month. Group Analytics adds 40% and Data Pipelines adds 20% to overage charges; Metric Trees, experiments/feature flags, account analytics, pipelines, and some support are add-ons.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Mixpanel, collect a small transparent event stream and build funnels and retention locally. The hard boundary is large-scale ingestion, identity handling, query engine, governance, and product expertise, plus data pipeline reliability and analytical depth.
coreLoopDIY: Collect a small transparent stream of privacy-conscious first-party events, build funnels and retention views locally, answer a small set of product questions, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
whatYouLose: large-scale ingestion, identity handling, query engine, governance, and product expertise
moatNotes: data pipeline reliability and analytical depth
ongoingBurden: event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Mixpanel because teams pay because analytics must keep collecting and remain trustworthy while the product changes underneath it. The recurring cost buys event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Umami
priorArt.desc: Popular open-source privacy-focused web analytics platform.

alternatives.name: OpenPanel
alternatives.desc: The useful product-analytics core, plus a ClickHouse stack you now get to know personally.

facts.install: Create a hosted account or run the self-host installer and Docker stack
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment uses PostgreSQL for account data, ClickHouse for event data and Redis for cache and queues; hosted data lives in OpenPanel's service
facts.gapVsPaid: Its query, cohort, retention, governance and integration ecosystem is less mature than Mixpanel's, and the free path brings ClickHouse operations.
facts.setupBlocker: None for the hosted free tier; self-hosting requires Docker, DNS or a reverse proxy and several persistent services

alternatives.name: PostHog
alternatives.desc: Funnels, cohorts and retention with a free million-event runway and considerably more machinery.

facts.install: Create a PostHog Cloud project or use the hobby self-host script on a Linux server
facts.dataFormat: The self-hosted stack splits analytics, transactions, queues and recordings across ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis and object storage; cloud data lives in PostHog's managed regions
facts.gapVsPaid: It is broader and heavier, with a less focused analytics interface and either usage quotas or a complex self-hosted stack.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted signup; self-hosting is an unsupported, resource-heavy multi-service stack requiring serious operations work

alternatives.name: Umami
alternatives.desc: Funnels, cohorts and retention locally, without the enterprise taxonomy workshop.

facts.install: Create an Umami Cloud account or deploy the Node application with Docker Compose and PostgreSQL
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment stores analytics and account data in PostgreSQL; Umami Cloud stores it in Umami's managed service
facts.gapVsPaid: Its identity, cohort, retention, governance and experimentation capabilities are far shallower than Mixpanel's.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted signup; self-hosting requires Docker or Node hosting and a PostgreSQL database

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Growth plan and a single-product first-party analytics DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Mixpanel in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: collect a small transparent stream of privacy-conscious first-party events, build funnels and retention views locally, answer a small set of product questions, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Ship a lightweight browser SDK for page views and explicit custom events.
Create projects, API keys, environments, event names, and a documented event schema.
Ingest idempotently, filter obvious bots, truncate IP data, and avoid fingerprinting.
Build dashboards for visitors, sessions, funnels, retention, sources, pages, and events.
Expose filters by date, environment, device, country, referrer, and selected properties.
Add retention controls, raw-event export, deletion, health checks, and backup instructions.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out cross-site identity graphs.
Deliberately leave out session replay and automatic DOM capture.
Deliberately leave out warehouse-scale reverse ETL and enterprise governance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
